recentes.titreEditorial: Measure who can actually use AI before you name an owner or buy a platform
The model ranking is a sales pitch, your in-house test is the only basis for a decision
The model changes weekly, your organisation must learn at the same pace
Your agents also serve those attacking you
The assistant that wrote now acts
AI on the phone, debt on the books
AI reaches the UN Security Council
Anthropic and OpenAI ship on the same day

More than twenty countries call for stronger human oversight of AI, without the United States, China or France, while Washington and Beijing open a warning channel between them ahead of the Trump-Xi summit. Google launches its Googlebook at $899 to sell Gemini, Meta's Muse agent races to the top of the charts before being blocked by Amazon and flagged for a security flaw, and British Columbia sues OpenAI after a mass shooting.

Charles III gathers AI bosses in Scotland and warns of \"existential dangers\", while a Pew survey across 37 countries shows a worldwide fear of job destruction. Brussels adopts the EU KIDS Act, Mistral moves into Firefox, Nvidia, Google and Anthropic join forces to find 100 gigawatts on the power grid, and Huawei pulls its next training chip forward by nine months to close the gap with Nvidia.

OpenAI admits six model misbehaviours and publishes a framework to report them, the same day Google opens the connected home to agents and Anthropic folds its interfaces into a single Claude that decides for itself how much work to take on. The agent moves from reading to acting. Meanwhile Brussels adopts the EU KIDS Act to keep minors off social media, Mistral arrives in Firefox, and Huawei pulls its next AI chip nine months forward to cut China's dependence on Nvidia.
Silicon Valley refuses to brake, Washington splits
AI leaders' call to slow down splits the world

AI leaders call for slowing the race, the White House refuses: Dario Amodei argues for \"pacing the frontier\", Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis agree, Donald Trump replies that he will not hand his lead to China, and Asian markets fall. Anthropic is eyeing the Nasdaq for a listing that could exceed $86 billion while OpenAI backs away from its own, SoftBank borrows $11.9 billion to fund OpenAI and Christine Lagarde warns about the financial cost of AI. In China, Z.ai returns to raise $5 billion in Hong Kong and the intelligence chief warns about the risks of AI.

AI safety moves from the activist fringe to mainstream debate: Sam Altman says he is ready to slow frontier AI development and is testing whether such a brake would be legal, a former Anthropic researcher warns that \"AI could kill us all,\" OpenAI adds a worried researcher to its board, and Anthropic publishes 161 pages of Claude misuse, from Yemeni missiles to fake dating profiles. In Europe, the CNIL sets rules for electronic invoicing and the EU's cybersecurity agency trials Anthropic's most offensive model. In China, DeepSeek reignites the price war with its V4.1 Flash model and chipmaker Enflame jumps 188% on its stock market debut. Microsoft plans 38 gigawatts of data centres and Jensen Huang promises Nvidia 70% growth.
Apple's first Ternus keynote and the OECD's student warning
OpenAI claims a Navier-Stokes proof, then a credit fight erupts

Mistral AI raises €3 billion at a €21 billion valuation in a round led by Samsung; the labor-law scholar Jean-Emmanuel Ray reminds employers that the AI Act requires them to inventory their high-risk AI systems and inform staff by the end of 2027, while BPCE stands up its AI Factory and Bercy renegotiates the French state's IT contracts; China targets 9,800 eflops of compute and Huawei launches its first stacked-circuit chip; Revolut completes the first AI-initiated payment in France

Moody's finds that Chinese companies get more compute per dollar spent than the US giants; the Seattle Times and Newsday sue OpenAI and Microsoft over copyright while the split of the Anthropic settlement pits authors against publishers; Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, describes an alien mind and calls for guardrails; and US job seekers hide instructions in their resumes to trick recruiters' AI
OpenAI ships GPT-6 Astra as three assistants go dark
Washington backs OpenAI against the New York Times
OpenAI rates Astra at critical cyber capability

The European Commission ranks ChatGPT among its most closely watched services under the DSA, the first generative AI targeted, OpenAI moves some of its large customers to performance-based billing, Anthropic signs $35 billion in compute with Lambda ahead of its IPO, and Nvidia invests $3.5 billion in MediaTek to stay indispensable

Sony Music and Warner sue Anthropic for \"one of the largest thefts of intellectual property in history\" on the eve of its stock market listing, Bill Gates calls for taxing machines, Google rolls out its AI answers by default at the expense of the blue links, and Caterpillar applies thirty years of mining automation to AI

Nvidia moves on Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, the open-source platform founded by three French entrepreneurs, the same week it was breached by OpenAI's agents; a federal judge overturns the Pentagon's ban on Anthropic, OpenAI brings advertising to ChatGPT in India, Zhipu unveils an open model trained on 100,000 Chinese chips, and OpenAI documents what critical thinking changes about using a chatbot

Nvidia posts a record $96.2 billion in quarterly revenue and looks ahead to 2028, while Amazon triples its chip order and Anthropic signs $45 billion of compute with Nscale; on the same day, OpenAI releases its report on the Hugging Face breach carried out by nearly 700 of its own agents, Bill Gates breaks his silence to call for a robot tax, and the CNIL updates its open-model traceability tool
Open-weight models pass proprietary ones on Vercel
Uber fined €825 million over automated decisions

Nvidia warns its biggest customers of a price rise above 15% on its AI servers as memory costs soar; the same day SoftBank places a record bond to fund OpenAI, Samsung returns $79 billion under the pressure of the AI boom, Alibaba raises $10.2 billion in Hong Kong, and Hugging Face is said to be exploring a sale at around $13 billion
Anthropic eyes a SpaceX-sized listing as enterprise buyers switch models
The AI Act makes provenance a job
OpenAI freezes part of Astra over cyber risk
Jeff Dean leaves Google as DeepMind reshuffles its command

edition.titreEditorial: Measure who can actually use AI before you name an owner or buy a platform
edition.chapeau: OpenAI dismisses three researchers from its safety teams over suspected leaks to an outside evaluation group, as the FTC prepares its first subpoenas. The same day, France launches its Arcadia project to take on Palantir over NATO's networks, Anthropic cuts off access to Claude from Hong Kong, and a PwC study shows that executives and technical leaders cannot say who, inside their own company, answers for AI risk.

une.titre: OpenAI removes three researchers from its safety teams, accused of sharing confidential information
une.texteHtml: The company ended its work with three researchers after an internal inquiry found several failures in the handling of sensitive information, according to the Wall Street Journal. One case involves material passed to an outside group tasked with evaluating the safety of AI models, exactly the kind of independent body meant to scrutinise the labs from the outside. The departure comes in a tense climate: the Federal Trade Commission, the US consumer protection authority, is looking into agents going off the rails and could issue its first subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic within a few weeks. The same month, tech bosses signed a "morally binding" self-regulation pact proposed by Donald Trump, with no legal force. For an organisation that relies on these models, the signal matters: outside verification of safety is tightening at the moment when usage is widening.

items.titre: France launches the Arcadia project to challenge the Americans over NATO's classified networks
items.texteHtml: Unveiled on 29 September, Arcadia aims to merge French military data on a large scale to gain an operational edge, Le Monde reports. The stakes go beyond the technology: at issue is the place of the American groups Palantir and Anduril in the modernisation of the Atlantic Alliance's structures, where France intends to offer a sovereign solution. The file squarely raises the question of who holds and processes European defence data.

items.titre: Airbus buys Quarkslab, the French firm that protects software against AI
items.texteHtml: The group completed on Thursday its acquisition of this cybersecurity company, known for QShield, a product that hardens software against AI-assisted analysis and reverse-engineering techniques, according to Clubic. The deal, announced in April, strengthens Airbus's cyber arm and keeps a sensitive software security component in Europe. It illustrates a quiet move by the continent's big industrial groups to consolidate France's cyber gems.

items.titre: Executives and technical leaders do not agree on who answers for AI risk, according to PwC
items.texteHtml: The firm's study highlights a growing need to designate a clear AI owner inside the company, failing which responsibility for incidents stays unassigned, ZDNet reports. Executives tend to send the subject back to the technical teams, who send it back to senior management. The gap widens at the moment when uses are multiplying and an agent going off the rails acts rather than merely writing.

items.titre: Pearson buys Workera to measure AI skills in the workplace
items.texteHtml: The publishing and training group has reached an agreement to acquire Workera, whose product assesses employees' real level of AI competence and directs training to where it is missing, ZDNet reports. The purchase makes the measurement of AI skills a market in its own right, separate from selling courses. For a management team, the logic flips: you first seek to know who can do what, before deciding what to teach.

items.titre: OpenAI and Meta push their agents to the general public for sensitive tasks
items.texteHtml: The two groups are trying to convince individuals to entrust their agents with actions more committing than mere writing, purchases and administrative steps included, Bloomberg writes. At its DevDay conference, OpenAI unveiled Dots, a "serious" agent powered by GPT-6 Astra, to answer Meta, whose agent platform Muse has had a noticed start, The Verge reports. The shift is clear: after the assistant that suggests comes the agent that executes and pays in your place. These tools, designed for individuals, will enter organisations through employees before any internal policy. The vendors' bet is that public trust will follow convenience; nothing guarantees it will follow as fast as the features.

items.titre: Albertsons rolls out ChatGPT Enterprise and the OpenAI API in its supermarkets
items.texteHtml: The US chain, one of the country's largest grocery retailers, says it uses these tools to speed up its teams' work and simplify the shopping of millions of customers, according to OpenAI, TechCrunch and ZDNet. The announcement matters less for the technical feat than for the scale: a mass-retail player is industrialising generative AI across its internal processes. This is the kind of documented rollout that gives a concrete measure of enterprise adoption, far from demos. It remains to be seen what quantified gains the retailer will publish once it has enough hindsight.

items.titre: Anthropic rents up to $42 billion of chips from Broadcom, Amazon moves $8 billion of servers off its balance sheet
items.texteHtml: Clubic describes a deal under which Anthropic commits to rent $42 billion of AI chips supplied by Broadcom, an example of those arrangements where the same players finance each other in a circle. The same day, Amazon is studying a transfer of around $8 billion of high-end Nvidia chips off its accounting balance sheet, according to the Financial Times as relayed by Bloomberg. The two operations tell the same strain: AI infrastructure costs so much that it pushes towards ever more acrobatic financial arrangements. For anyone buying AI services, these tens-of-billions commitments end up weighing on the price billed.

items.titre: A federal judge dismisses the antitrust complaints against Google's AI Overviews
items.texteHtml: Judge Amit Mehta threw out two actions filed by Chegg and Penske Media, parent company of Rolling Stone, which accused Google of capturing web traffic with its AI-generated search summaries, according to The Verge, citing Reuters. The ruling sides with Google on this specific ground. For the publishers who see their audience shrink as search engines answer in place of websites, the legal route closes and leaves the economic problem untouched.

items.titre: Anthropic tightens access to Claude from Hong Kong, including via VPN
items.texteHtml: Many Hong Kong users saw their account suspended without notice after connecting through a virtual private network (VPN), a tool that hides the real location, the South China Morning Post reports. A wave of complaints appeared on Thursday on X and Reddit, from accounts active for months. Anthropic applies geographic restrictions to its models, and is strengthening its detection of workarounds. The measure is a reminder that access to the big American models depends on a shifting political map, and that a team based in a restricted zone can lose its tool overnight.

items.titre: Washington tightens its grip on Nvidia chips diverted to China
items.texteHtml: Federal prosecutors arrested on Thursday a Californian accused of shipping to China servers containing $300 million of Nvidia chips, in violation of export controls, according to Bloomberg. In parallel, a financing company owned by several Chinese local authorities documented the purchase of Blackwell chips that are nonetheless restricted, a sign of public support for trade that Washington deems illicit. The two cases show export controls that hold poorly: the hardware gets through despite the barriers, and players tied to the Chinese state organise its acquisition. The question put to the US authorities is why the warning signs were not seen earlier.

items.titre: An AI tool reconstructs what you are looking at from a brain scan
items.texteHtml: Researchers describe in MIT Technology Review a model able to guess the image a person is viewing by analysing their brain activity, then recreate it with notable accuracy. The system also works in reverse: predicting brain activity from the image being viewed. The published demonstrations compare the real image and its reconstruction, often close. Beyond the feat, the work raises concrete questions about protecting the most intimate data there is, that of neural activity, as imaging and AI move closer together.

• Grok reportedly advised Donald Trump to capture Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, the head of state having sought the opinion of Elon Musk's chatbot before an operation, according to a TechCrunch article presented as a report not confirmed by those involved. TechCrunch
  • The Opus 5.5 model betrays its writing through the word "dependable", twenty-three times more frequent than in human texts, according to an analysis of AI stylistic tells noted by TechCrunch. TechCrunch
  • Carried by Mistral AI, French Tech records its biggest month of fundraising since 2023, Maddyness reports.

analyse.titre: PwC shows that executives and technical leaders pass AI risk back and forth without deciding, on the day Pearson buys Workera to measure employees' AI skills and \"citizen developers\" build applications with agents: what changes for a French organisation is that the scarce resource is no longer access to the tool but an honest map of who can actually do what with it, and the concrete lever is to measure real AI skill through a test on your own tasks, not on self-reporting, then make it a line in the job description rather than a side project.
analyse.these: The scarce resource is no longer access to the models, which are becoming commonplace, but an honest map of who, inside the organisation, can do what with them; the move that sets a French company apart is to measure its teams' real AI skill through a test on their own tasks, write it into the job descriptions, and base adoption and governance on that proof, before naming an owner or buying a platform.
analyse.html:
PwC asked companies a simple question: who, inside your organisation, answers for AI risk? Executives point to the technical leadership, technical leaders point back to senior management, and the firm concludes there is a glaring need to finally designate an owner. The same day, Pearson buys Workera, whose business is to measure employees' real level of AI competence. Put these two facts together, add the "citizen developers" that the Journal du Net sees building applications with agents without going through the IT department, and a signal emerges. What is becoming scarce inside the organisation is no longer access to the models, now ordinary and cheap, but an honest map of who can actually do what with them.

As long as that map does not exist, two failures are in the making. You name an AI owner without knowing what the teams can do, and the post becomes a lightning rod with no grip on the ground. You buy a platform or a training plan calibrated on assumed skills, declared in an internal survey, never verified. Self-reporting always lies in the same direction: everyone thinks they are at ease with a tool they barely touch.

The move that sets a French company apart comes down to a measurement, not an org chart. Take fifteen real tasks from your lines of business, a contract to review, a customer reply to draft, a spreadsheet to analyse, and have a sample of employees handle them with and without AI. You get an observed skill, not a feeling. Then write it into the job descriptions, on the same footing as a language or a piece of software, so it is maintained and assessed. Governance will follow, because you only entrust a scope of actions to people whose level you know.

The wave of consumer agents from OpenAI and Meta will enter your walls through employees, whether a policy allows it or not. The company that has measured before deciding will keep control. The others will discover their skills on the day of an incident.

The Masteria editorial team.
